openers.hist: In 1972 delegates from around the world met in Stockholm for the first global conference on environmental issues. The ideas they argued over were much older. In 18th-century France the physiocrats held that a nation's wealth comes solely from its land, and the British classical economists who followed thought hard about land, labor and limits. This last part of the course traces how those threads came together: in books like Rachel Carson's Silent Spring, in the Brundtland Report's definition of sustainable development, and in the summits from Rio de Janeiro to Johannesburg. It also meets the people and institutions, from the Club of Rome to the TEEB study, who tried to put a price on what nature does for us.
openers.how-the-field-developed: Economists were thinking about nature long before anyone spoke of an environmental movement. Physiocracy, whose name means 'government of nature', was an 18th-century French theory that all wealth comes from land and farming. Two centuries later, the conservation movement, Silent Spring in 1962 and the first Earth Day in 1970 pushed nature onto the political agenda. The 1972 Stockholm conference, the 1987 Brundtland Report and the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio turned that pressure into a global project. This chapter follows that path, from the ideas of Adam Smith's era to the TEEB study's effort to show what losing biodiversity costs.

reviews.how-the-field-developed: The story of this chapter runs on two tracks that slowly converge. On one, economists from the physiocrats and Malthus to Pigou and Krutilla asked how land, population, side effects and wild places fit into the economy. On the other, writers and activists, from Leopold and Carson to the Ehrlichs and Schumacher, warned that growth was eating into nature's limits. The two tracks met in Stockholm in 1972, where governments agreed that Earth's capacity to produce vital renewable resources must be kept. From there, the Brundtland Report, the Rio summits and the TEEB and Dasgupta studies tried to make nature count in the language economists and governments use, while critics kept asking whether a price can ever say what nature is worth.

nature-hist-002.title: Stockholm 1972: the world's first environment summit
nature-hist-002.text: It took four years, 114 governments and over $30,000,000 just to prepare. Sweden had proposed the idea to the UN's Economic and Social Council in 1968. The result was the United Nations Conference on the Human Environment, held in Stockholm from 5 to 16 June 1972, the first global conference on environmental issues. It is the moment when {{ref:nature-found-023}} became a matter for diplomats. The meeting agreed a Declaration of 26 principles, an Action Plan of 109 recommendations and a Resolution. It also created {{ref:nature-hist-031}}, the first UN agency headquartered in a developing country, in Nairobi. The meeting was not harmonious. Developing countries made up 70 of the 122 countries attending, and divisions between rich and poor surfaced quickly, while the Soviet bloc stayed away in protest. India's Indira Gandhi gave a speech linking the care of nature with relieving poverty, and that link became one of the conference's central themes. At home, the conference spurred countries to monitor their environments and set up environment ministries and agencies. Its long shadow is easy to trace. The 1992 {{ref:nature-hist-003}}, the 2002 Johannesburg summit and {{ref:nature-hist-008}} in 2012 all took its {{ref:nature-hist-015}} as their starting point.

nature-hist-003.title: Rio 1992: the Earth Summit and its treaties
nature-hist-003.text: In June 1992, 108 heads of state and government gathered in Rio de Janeiro. The Earth Summit, formally the United Nations Conference on Environment and Development, ran from 3 to 14 June. It built directly on {{ref:nature-hist-002}} twenty years earlier, and it did more than any meeting before it to spread the idea of {{ref:nature-eecon-209}}. Its biggest achievement was the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, signed by 154 states, which later led to the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement. The Convention on Biological Diversity was opened for signature there too. The summit also produced the Rio Declaration and Agenda 21, a plan of action. In all, 178 governments voted to adopt them, and a Commission on Sustainable Development was set up to oversee them. Rio helped spread three principles that run through later treaties. The precautionary principle says to act against serious threats even before the science is complete. Common but differentiated responsibilities means all countries share the duty but not equally. The polluter pays principle puts the cost of pollution on whoever causes it. Not everyone was impressed. Critics note that many Rio promises on poverty and cleanup were never kept, and some leaders called the whole effort green imperialism by the global North.

nature-hist-012.title: Classical economics: Smith, Ricardo, Malthus and Mill
nature-hist-012.text: In 1776 Adam Smith published The Wealth of Nations, and a new way of thinking about the economy began. Classical economics is the school of thought that flourished mainly in Britain from the late 18th to the mid-19th century. Its leaders were Smith, David Ricardo, Thomas Malthus and John Stuart Mill. These thinkers founded {{ref:nature-found-044}} as we know it. They saw markets as largely self-regulating, a view summed up in Smith's image of the {{ref:nature-econ-387}}. For Smith, a nation's wealth was its yearly income. Labor, land and capital produced it, and it was shared out as wages, rent and profits. Land, in other words, sat at the heart of the system. The classical economists favored free trade over the protectionism of the earlier mercantilists. Ricardo explained trade's gains through comparative advantage: each country does best by specializing in what it gives up least to produce. Mill went further than the others in a direction that sounds modern. He believed a future 'stationary state', with constant population and capital, was both inevitable and desirable, an idea now called a steady-state economy. Not everyone admired the school. Thomas Carlyle nicknamed it 'the dismal science', a jibe often linked to Malthus's gloomy analysis. From the 1870s it gave way to neoclassical economics, though many of its ideas remain fundamental.

nature-hist-004.title: Our Common Future: defining sustainable development
nature-hist-004.text: Nine hundred days of public hearings and expert testimony, held around the world, produced one famous sentence. Our Common Future, better known as the Brundtland Report, is the October 1987 report of the UN's World Commission on Environment and Development. Former Norwegian Prime Minister Gro Harlem Brundtland chaired the work, which is why the body is often called the {{ref:nature-eecon-222}}. Its sentence defined {{ref:nature-eecon-209}} as development that meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. The report treated environment and development as one single issue rather than two. It stressed that economic, environmental and social sides of human development lock together. Poverty, it argued, worsens pressure on the environment, and there are environmental limits to economic growth. Fifteen years after {{ref:nature-hist-002}}, it laid the groundwork for the 1992 Earth Summit, Agenda 21 and the Rio Declaration. Its reception was not universal applause. In 1988 the scholar Helge Ole Bergesen wrote that Third World elites saw the report as green imperialism.

nature-hist-014.title: The conservation movement: saving resources for later
nature-hist-014.text: In 1662 John Evelyn's book Sylva urged England to slow the felling of its trees and replant the ones it cut. The conservation movement is often traced to that plea. It is an environmental, social and political movement that seeks to manage and protect {{ref:nature-res-248}}s, wild species and their habitats for the future. It grew from practical need: people wanted to keep their fisheries, wildlife, water, soil and forests going. By the 19th century it had an ethic. Human activity harms the environment, people have a civic duty to keep it for future generations, and science should guide that duty. The first practical use of scientific conservation came in the forests of India in the mid-19th century. Over time the goals widened. Conservation moved from steady yields of resources and the preservation of wilderness to the protection of biodiversity, the whole variety of living things. Its history has a darker side. Scholars note that early conservation often protected game for elite white hunters while policing hunting by Indigenous and poor people.

nature-hist-006.title: Silent Spring: the book that turned the US against DDT
nature-hist-006.text: Rachel Carson thought the word pesticide was too kind. In Silent Spring, her 1962 book, she argued that these chemicals should be called 'biocides', because their effects rarely stop at the target pests. The book documented the harm done by indiscriminate use of the pesticide DDT and its spread through the wider environment as {{ref:nature-found-079}}. Carson accused the chemical industry of spreading disinformation and officials of accepting its claims without question. Chemical companies fought back hard. They lost the argument with the public. Silent Spring shifted opinion, reversed US pesticide policy and led to a national ban on DDT for farm use. It also fed the movement that created the US Environmental Protection Agency. The book became a rallying point for the new social movement of the 1960s and is seen as the start of the deep ecology movement. As one scholar put it, after Carson no one could so easily sell pollution as the necessary underside of progress. A dispute still clings to it. Some anti-environmentalist groups blame Carson for malaria deaths after DDT was restricted. Scientists and journalists have dismissed that claim as a myth, but it has not gone away.

nature-hist-008.title: Rio+20: the summit that called for new global goals
nature-hist-008.text: Twenty years after the {{ref:nature-hist-003}}, the world came back to the same city. Rio+20, the United Nations Conference on Sustainable Development, ran from 13 to 22 June 2012 and tried to reconcile economic and environmental goals. It had two themes: a green economy that lifts people out of poverty, and an institutional framework for sustainable development. Its 49-page outcome document, 'The Future We Want', was nonbinding. It called for the Sustainable Development Goals, a set of measurable targets. Nations agreed to explore alternatives to GDP that count things like nature's carbon storage, and reaffirmed promises to phase out fossil fuel subsidies. The summit also popularized the term blue economy. Yet Obama, Merkel and Cameron stayed away, a sign that sustainability was not their priority.

nature-hist-026.title: The Club of Rome and The Limits to Growth
nature-hist-026.text: Its first report sold 30 million copies in more than 30 languages, the best-selling environmental book in history. The Club of Rome is an informal non-profit group of intellectuals and business leaders, founded in Rome in 1968. Italian industrialist Aurelio Peccei and British scientist Alexander King started it because they doubted that technology and development alone could solve the world's problems. That 1972 report was {{ref:nature-eecon-154}}. Its computer simulations suggested that growth in production and consumption could not go on forever, because resources would run out or pollution would build up. The OECD, committed to unfettered growth, reacted with hostility. Critics remain divided. Economist Robert Solow called the scenarios 'simplistic', and a 1973 Sussex University study, Models of Doom, found the forecasts hinged on a few unduly pessimistic assumptions. Yet in 2009 Solow allowed that rapid growth in India and China might change the picture. The club has issued 55 reports, including 'Earth for All' in 2022.

nature-hist-016.title: Earth Day: a teach-in that became a global event
nature-hist-016.text: In 1969 an oil spill off Santa Barbara released over 3 million US gallons of oil and killed more than 10,000 seabirds and sea mammals. US Senator Gaylord Nelson was moved to act. He proposed a nationwide environmental teach-in for April 22, 1970, and hired a young activist, Denis Hayes, to run it. That was the first Earth Day, now an annual event in support of environmental protection. The decade that followed brought the Clean Air and Clean Water Acts, the EPA, and bans on DDT and leaded gasoline. In 1990 Earth Day went global, mobilizing 200 million people in 141 countries. In 2016, leaders of 175 nations signed the Paris Agreement on Earth Day. Nelson summed up its view: 'The economy is a wholly owned subsidiary of the environment, not the other way around.'

nature-hist-017.title: Physiocracy: when wealth came only from the land
nature-hist-017.text: Its name, from the Greek, means 'government of nature'. Physiocracy was an 18th-century French theory holding that a nation's wealth comes solely from its land and farming. Led by François Quesnay, the Marquis de Mirabeau and Turgot, it was one of the first well-developed theories in {{ref:nature-found-044}}, just before Adam Smith. Unlike the mercantilists, who counted a ruler's gold, the physiocrats saw productive work as the source of wealth. But only farm labor created value; industry was an 'unproductive appendage' to agriculture. They trusted a 'natural order' and laissez-faire, the idea that self-interest and free trade make an economy work. Turgot saw diminishing returns: adding more of one input raises output at a falling rate, so wealth cannot grow without limit. Smith, Ricardo, Mill and Henry George all drew on them.

nature-hist-001.title: TEEB: putting a price on the loss of nature
nature-hist-001.text: Deforestation and degradation were costing the world US$2–4.5 trillion of natural capital a year, by TEEB's 2008 estimate. The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity was an international study, led by {{ref:nature-hist-047}} from 2007 to 2011. It set out to show the global economic benefits of {{ref:nature-found-001}} and the rising cost of {{ref:nature-eco-035}}. Germany and the European Commission launched it after G8+5 environment ministers asked for such a study at Potsdam. It found that US$45 billion a year spent on protected areas could secure {{ref:nature-found-004}}s worth some US$5 trillion a year. Values ranged from about $100 per hectare per year for open ocean to over $1,000,000 for the richest coral reefs. Its second phase was presented in Nagoya, Japan, in October 2010. Critics doubt that values based on human preferences can tell us what nature must be kept to sustain life.

nature-hist-009.title: Johannesburg 2002: Rio+10 and its partnerships
nature-hist-009.text: Ten years after the {{ref:nature-hist-003}}, the World Summit on Sustainable Development met in Johannesburg, South Africa, from 26 August to 4 September 2002. There, {{ref:nature-eecon-209}} was recognized as an overarching goal for institutions at every level. Instead of new treaties, it produced almost 300 'partnership initiatives' aimed at the Millennium Development Goals, plus the Johannesburg Declaration. US President George W. Bush boycotted the summit, which left it partly impotent.

nature-hist-019.title: Small Is Beautiful: economics as if people mattered
nature-hist-019.text: A modern economy that burns fossil fuels is spending its savings and calling it income. That was {{ref:nature-hist-060}}'s charge in Small Is Beautiful: A Study of Economics As If People Mattered, a 1973 essay collection. He argued that mainstream {{ref:nature-found-044}} ignores nature's limits. Resources such as oil are {{ref:nature-found-010}} that will run out, and nature's ability to absorb pollution is limited too. His philosophy of 'enoughness' grew from studying village economies, which he called Buddhist economics. The title came from his teacher Leopold Kohr, who made the case for small, appropriate technologies over 'bigger is better'. The book inspired the appropriate technology movement. The 1973 energy crisis helped it find a wide audience, and in 1995 it was ranked among the 100 most influential books since World War II.

nature-hist-005.title: A Sand County Almanac and the land ethic
nature-hist-005.text: Little noticed when it appeared in 1949, the book of essays by {{ref:nature-hist-051}} became a surprise bestseller in the 1970s. Over two million copies have now been printed. A Sand County Almanac argues for a {{ref:nature-val-049}}, a responsible relationship between people and the land. Its rule is simple: a thing is right when it tends to preserve the integrity, stability and beauty of the living community, and wrong when it does not. Leopold insisted land is not a commodity to be owned. He objected that policy makers always need an economic motive before they will conserve. His essay 'Thinking Like a Mountain' shows how killing top predators such as wolves ripples through a whole ecosystem. A 1990 poll ranked the book with Silent Spring as the two most significant environmental books of the 20th century.

nature-hist-011.title: Malthus and the race between people and food
nature-hist-011.text: Thomas Robert Malthus published An Essay on the Principle of Population in 1798. His argument was that population tends to grow until it outruns food and other basic resources, a race between {{ref:nature-econ-442}} and limited supply. In good times numbers expand until they are too large for the land to feed. Two checks then hold them back. Preventive checks lower births, through delayed marriage for example. Positive checks raise deaths, through hunger, disease and war. Malthus also tied population to wages: as workers multiply faster than food, food costs rise, real wages fall, and growth slows. Darwin and Wallace both credited him with helping them see natural selection. Whether his limits hold is disputed. Critics such as Julian Simon point out that huge 20th-century population growth brought no catastrophe, thanks to better farming.

nature-hist-020.title: The Population Bomb: a famine forecast that missed
nature-hist-020.text: Hundreds of millions would starve to death in the 1970s whatever was done. So began The Population Bomb, a 1968 book by Paul and Anne Ehrlich calling for immediate limits on population growth. Critics saw it as a restatement of {{ref:nature-hist-011}}. The famines did not come. The global death rate fell from 13 per 1000 in 1965–74 to 10 per 1000 in 1985–90, while calories per person rose 24%. Julian Simon and Hans Rosling argued the book wrongly assumed growth would continue with no technological or social progress. Barry Commoner argued that helping poor people grow richer would lower birth rates on its own. Opinion is still split. The Ehrlichs stand by their core claim that population growth is a major problem, and supporters say the book brought human numbers into environmental debate.

nature-hist-015.title: The Stockholm Declaration's 26 principles
nature-hist-015.text: People have a right to an environment that allows a life of dignity and well-being, and a duty to protect it for present and future generations. So says the first principle of the Stockholm Declaration, the first UN declaration on the global environment, agreed at the {{ref:nature-hist-002}}. Among its 26 principles, it says Earth's capacity to produce vital renewable resources must be kept and, where practicable, restored. Principle 21, its legal core, gives states sovereign rights over their own territory along with a duty not to harm others across borders. Developing countries argued that rich nations used most resources and caused most pollution, so the Global North should bear most of the responsibility. Indira Gandhi's line that 'poverty is the worst form of pollution' framed a North–South divide that lasted decades. The declaration is not legally binding, and critics found much of it vague. Still, the 1992 Rio Declaration adopted a modified Principle 21.

nature-hist-022.title: Mercantilism: the race to hoard gold
nature-hist-022.text: For mercantilists, money and precious metals were the only true riches. Mercantilism is a nationalist economic policy that aims to maximize a country's exports and minimize its imports, using tariffs to tip the balance. Its followers believed trade could not benefit all countries at once: one nation's gain was another's loss. It dominated modernizing Europe from the 16th to the 19th centuries. Adam Smith vigorously opposed it and argued for free trade.

nature-hist-021.title: From philosophy to economics: a short history
nature-hist-021.text: Until the Industrial Revolution, economics in the West was a branch of philosophy rather than a subject of its own. The history of economic thought studies its thinkers and theories. {{ref:nature-hist-022}} dominated Europe from the 16th to the 18th century, until the physiocrats and then Adam Smith challenged it. Neoclassical economics arose in the 1870s in three independent schools, at Cambridge, in Austria and in Lausanne. In 1920 {{ref:nature-hist-038}} argued that markets fail when there are side effects on others, so the state must step in. In the 1930s economists began modeling how to manage resources that run out. Long before, Malthus on overpopulation and Mill on the stationary state had anticipated the worries of {{ref:nature-eecon-059}}, founded in the work of Boulding, Georgescu-Roegen and Daly.

nature-hist-013.title: Natural price: the classical theory of value
nature-hist-013.text: Market prices bounce around, but the classical economists believed something steadier lay underneath. Their theory of value explained prices by a 'natural price', set by lasting forces, toward which day-to-day prices tend to move. William Petty first separated the two. Adam Smith said market prices are drawn toward natural prices somewhat like gravity, and that the natural price was the sum of natural wages, profits and rent. Petty grounded value in land and labor. How this theory relates to later economics is still debated.

nature-hist-018.title: Quesnay's Tableau économique: the economy as a body
nature-hist-018.text: François Quesnay was a physician, and he saw wealth moving through a nation the way blood moves through a body. His Tableau économique, described in 1759, traced how production and money flow between three classes. Landowners formed one. Farm workers were the 'productive' class. Artisans and merchants were the 'sterile' class. This early economic model came out of {{ref:nature-hist-017}}. It holds the origins of modern ideas about how wealth circulates and how the parts of an economy depend on one another.

nature-hist-028.title: The Dasgupta Review: we are living on 1.6 Earths
nature-hist-028.text: To support current living standards, humanity would need 1.6 Earths. That was one finding of a 2021 report on the economics of biodiversity, led by the economist {{ref:nature-hist-046}} and commissioned by the British Treasury. Published in February 2021, it found biodiversity declining faster than at any time in human history. Human demands, it argued, far exceed nature's capacity to supply the goods and services we rely on. It called for changes on the scale of the Marshall Plan or bigger, including abandoning GDP as the measure of economic success. The review advocated thinking of nature as {{ref:nature-found-010}}. In June 2021 the UK government responded by committing to a nature-positive future. Not everyone was persuaded: ecological economist Clive Spash published critical deconstructions of it.

nature-hist-024.title: The Economics of Welfare: Pigou's tax on harm
nature-hist-024.text: The Economics of Welfare, a 1920 book by {{ref:nature-hist-038}}, introduced the idea of the {{ref:nature-found-031}}. That is a cost or benefit that falls on others, which the person causing it does not account for. Pigou built on an idea of his teacher Alfred Marshall. His argument was that markets are inefficient when such side effects exist, so the state must step in. The book first planted the idea that governments should tax activities that put uncompensated costs on others, now called a {{ref:nature-pol-088}}. Pigou applied the reasoning to traffic jams, an early case of congestion pricing.

nature-hist-025.title: Conservation Reconsidered: valuing what we never use
nature-hist-025.text: Some people value a wild river they will never see. A 1967 paper by {{ref:nature-hist-041}}, Conservation Reconsidered, described the economic value of undisturbed places such as rivers and forests. In it he introduced {{ref:nature-val-054}}, the value people get from the mere existence of something, such as unspoiled wilderness or a species, even if they never use it. This idea of 'nonuse value' made its author a pioneer of environmental economics.
